Foundations of a Time-Consistent Counterfactual
Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents
Foundational working paper

Hao-Hsuan Chen Affiliation: Department of Risk Management and Insurance Affiliation: National Chengchi University Email: dannychen9199@gmail.com
May 2026
Abstract

We propose a foundational runtime actuarial layer for autonomous AI agents in which every side-effect-bearing action carries a time-consistent, counterfactual risk toll computed against a contractually fixed safe default, inside an explicit underwriting boundary. The framework treats per-action insurance as the primary unit of analysis and replaces post-hoc annual liability cover with a pre-action transaction layer. The paper establishes four structural results: (i) a well-defined counterfactual toll under a chosen safe-default mapping and continuation policy, with explicit non-uniqueness; (ii) a no-splitting property within an underwriting boundary that telescopes path-decomposed actions into a boundary potential, with a corollary tying gaming-resistance to boundary design; (iii) an irreversible-authority premium, split into a strictly positive action-level component and an if-and-only-if characterisation of the set-level robust capital increase; and (iv) a conservative runtime gating theorem that translates high-probability toll envelopes into an executed-action budget guarantee. The result is the mathematical base layer for a broader program: an empirical companion instantiates the runtime through an Actuarial Action Interface and authority-frontier experiments; a mechanism-design companion studies strategic operator incentives and cross-boundary aggregation; and a dynamic-underwriting companion studies experience rating and audit-replay calibration. The present paper states the primitive contract, the toll identity, the within-boundary no-arbitrage result, and the budget guarantee on which those later layers depend.

1 Positioning

The research question is:

How can insurance, warranty, or escrow-backed guarantees be embedded directly into an autonomous AI agent runtime, so that each economically meaningful action is priced, budgeted, and gated before execution?

The intended contribution is not another audit score for AI systems. The object is a transaction layer: every side-effect-bearing action pays a risk toll, or it is blocked, downgraded to a safe default, or escalated to human approval.

This paper deliberately avoids three common traps.

  1. 1.

    Static tail-risk allocation is not new. Euler allocation, marginal expected shortfall, and expected-shortfall capital attribution are standard tools [20, 1, 14]. The novelty here is the dynamic, action-conditioned, runtime object, not the use of a coherent risk measure.

  2. 2.

    Conditional CVaR is not automatically time-consistent. Runtime decisions require a dynamic risk measure compatible with Bellman’s principle, not a naive sequence of one-period CVaR calculations [16, 6, 17].

  3. 3.

    Agent actions are not tokens. The unit of pricing is a side-effect-bearing tool call with external economic, legal, or operational consequences, not internal chain-of-thought, hidden deliberation, or token generation.

Role in the research program.

This paper is the foundation layer. It defines the priced object (a side-effect-bearing action), the counterfactual comparison (execute the action versus execute the safe default), the aggregation unit (an underwriting boundary), and the pathwise budget guarantee. Later layers use these objects without changing them: the empirical runtime layer [7] implements the gate and measures authority release; the mechanism-design layer asks which contract clauses make strategic manipulation unprofitable; and the dynamic-underwriting layer asks how premiums and reserves should update as experience accumulates. This separation is deliberate: Paper A proves the primitive actuarial accounting identities, while companion work tests, extends, and strategically hardens them.

2 Related Work

Algorithmic and AI insurance.

Bertsimas and Orfanoudaki [4] price liability exposure for machine-driven classification decisions and connect model properties to insurance value; Bertsimas et al. [5] extends adaptive robust optimisation to catastrophe pricing. Recent work on trustworthy AI agents proposes transaction-level compensation and underwriting-inspired standards for agent-mediated transactions [12]. This paper differs by making the priced object an individual side-effect action inside a runtime control loop, rather than an annual policy or product warranty.

Dynamic risk measures.

Time consistency is central. Conditional CVaR and VaR can fail dynamic consistency in multistage settings [16, 13]. Dynamic coherent or convex risk measures restore a version of Bellman’s principle through recursive conditional risk mappings [6, 8, 10, 17, 18]. Risk-sensitive Markov decision processes provide the algorithmic counterpart [9, 19].

Causal credit assignment.

The proposed toll is counterfactual: it compares the loss distribution under executing an action with the loss distribution under a safe default using an interventional model [15]. In deployed systems, the interventional distribution can be approximated by simulator rollouts, causal world models, or off-policy estimators.

Runtime guarantees.

The implementation goal is not exact real-time tail-risk computation for every action. It is conservative gating: fast upper bounds for routine actions, and deeper simulation or human escalation for high-stakes actions. Conformal prediction can provide finite-sample high-probability upper envelopes under specified calibration assumptions [21, 2]; online adaptive selection requires adaptive variants [11].

3 Model

3.1 Histories and side-effect actions

Fix a finite horizon TT. Let (Ω,ℱ,(ℱt)t=0T,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T},\mathbb{P}) be a filtered probability space with ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} trivial. At time tt the agent has history ht∈ℋth_{t}\in\mathcal{H}_{t} represented by ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, and selects at∈𝒜t​(ht)a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}).

Definition 1 (Side-effect-bearing action).

Decompose the environment state at time tt as st=(stint,stext)s_{t}=(s_{t}^{\mathrm{int}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}}), where stexts_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}} collects contractually designated external state components such as financial ledgers, persistent databases, third-party communications, legal commitments, security permissions, and production systems. An action a∈𝒜t​(ht)a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}) is side-effect-bearing relative to an underwriting boundary if the interventional transition kernel of st+1exts_{t+1}^{\mathrm{ext}} under do⁡(a)\operatorname{do}(a) differs from the kernel under the null (or contractually identified no-op) action on at least one designated external component, and the induced change is not freely and instantaneously reversible by the agent alone within contractually specified time and cost thresholds. Examples: payment, refund, order placement, database write, email send, form submission, code deployment, trade execution, claim adjudication. Internal reasoning, hidden deliberation, and token generation are not priced actions.

Definition 2 (Minimal-authority safe default).

For an intended action a∈𝒜t​(ht)a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}), the safe default at0​(ht)a^{0}_{t}(h_{t}) is the ex ante fixed, least externally committing action in 𝒜t​(ht)\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}) that preserves the same intent while minimising external authority. The mapping a↦at0​(ht)a\mapsto a^{0}_{t}(h_{t}) is part of the contract and cannot be selected by the operator after observing the toll; this prevents the adversary from picking the safe default that minimises its own counterfactual gap. Examples: “send email” ↦\mapsto “save draft”; “execute trade” ↦\mapsto “paper trade”; “pay invoice” ↦\mapsto “draft payment for approval”; “drop table” ↦\mapsto “log proposed change without execution”.

3.2 Counterfactual losses

Let L∈L+p​(ℱT)L\in L^{p}_{+}(\mathcal{F}_{T}), p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], be terminal loss. For an intervention do⁡(a)\operatorname{do}(a) at history hth_{t}, let Ldo⁡(a),π+L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}} denote terminal loss when action aa is forced at time tt and a fixed continuation policy π+\pi^{+} is followed thereafter. We make the continuation policy explicit in notation throughout. The interventional distribution may be supplied by:

  1. 1.

    a sandbox simulator (reference implementation in companion Paper B);

  2. 2.

    a causal world model st+1=f⁡(st,at,ξt)s_{t+1}=f(s_{t},a_{t},\xi_{t});

  3. 3.

    an off-policy estimator from logged trajectories.

Assumption 3 (Interventional well-posedness).

For each priced action a∈𝒜t​(ht)a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}) and safe default at0​(ht)a^{0}_{t}(h_{t}), the interventional terminal losses Ldo⁡(a),π+L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}} and Ldo⁡(at0​(ht)),π+L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}_{t}(h_{t})),\pi^{+}} are well-defined elements of L+p​(ℱT)L^{p}_{+}(\mathcal{F}_{T}) under an admissible family of environment models ℳ\mathcal{M}.

3.3 Time-consistent dynamic risk

Let σt:Lp​(ℱt+1)→Lp​(ℱt)\sigma_{t}:L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{t+1})\to L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{t}) be a one-step conditional risk mapping. The dynamic risk process is defined recursively:

ρT(X)=X,ρt(X)=σt(ρt+1(X)),t=T−1,…,0.\rho_{T}(X)=X,\qquad\rho_{t}(X)=\sigma_{t}\bigl(\rho_{t+1}(X)\bigr),\quad t=T-1,\ldots,0. (1)
Assumption 4 (Convex, time-consistent runtime risk).

Each one-step mapping σt\sigma_{t} satisfies, for all X,Y∈Lp​(ℱt+1)X,Y\in L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{t+1}) and ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable bounded mm:

  1. (i)

    (normalisation) σt​(0)=0\sigma_{t}(0)=0;

  2. (ii)

    (monotonicity) X≤Y⇒σt​(X)≤σt​(Y)X\leq Y\Rightarrow\sigma_{t}(X)\leq\sigma_{t}(Y);

  3. (iii)

    (locality) σt​(𝟏A​X)=𝟏A​σt​(X)\sigma_{t}(\mathbf{1}_{A}X)=\mathbf{1}_{A}\sigma_{t}(X) for A∈ℱtA\in\mathcal{F}_{t};

  4. (iv)

    (translation invariance) σt​(X+m)=σt​(X)+m\sigma_{t}(X+m)=\sigma_{t}(X)+m;

  5. (v)

    (convexity) σt​(λ​X+(1−λ)​Y)≤λ​σt​(X)+(1−λ)​σt​(Y)\sigma_{t}(\lambda X+(1-\lambda)Y)\leq\lambda\sigma_{t}(X)+(1-\lambda)\sigma_{t}(Y), λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1].

Coherent specialisations additionally impose positive homogeneity σt​(λ​X)=λ​σt​(X)\sigma_{t}(\lambda X)=\lambda\sigma_{t}(X) for λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 [3]. The entropic special case σt​(Y)=γ−1​log⁡𝔼⁡[exp⁡(γ​Y)∣ℱt]\sigma_{t}(Y)=\gamma^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}[\exp(\gamma Y)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}], γ>0\gamma>0, satisfies (i)–(v) and yields a time-consistent recursive composition, but is not coherent because positive homogeneity fails in general. We use the entropic family as the reference runtime mapping throughout; results below require only the convex case unless explicitly stated.

3.4 Underwriting boundary

Definition 5 (Underwriting boundary).

An underwriting boundary B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B} is a contractually defined unit of aggregation, e.g.

B=(legal entity,rolling time window,action category,currency or asset class).B=(\text{legal entity},\;\text{rolling time window},\;\text{action category},\;\text{currency or asset class}).

Let EtB∈ℝ+dE^{B}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{+} be the observable cumulative exposure state inside BB at time tt, and let Δ​EtB​(at)∈ℝ+d\Delta E^{B}_{t}(a_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{+} be the exposure increment contributed by action ata_{t}.

Assumption 6 (Boundary observability).

For each boundary BB, the cumulative exposure EtBE^{B}_{t} and increment Δ​EtB​(at)\Delta E^{B}_{t}(a_{t}) are observable, contractually attributable, and updated before the next action priced in BB is evaluated.

4 Counterfactual Action Toll

Definition 7 (Counterfactual action toll).

Given history hth_{t}, continuation policy π+\pi^{+}, dynamic risk process ρt\rho_{t}, and safe-default mapping a0a^{0}, the action-level counterfactual risk toll is

ct​(a∣ht;π+,ρ,a0)=ρt​(Ldo⁡(a),π+)−ρt​(Ldo⁡(at0​(ht)),π+).c_{t}(a\mid h_{t};\pi^{+},\rho,a^{0})\;=\;\rho_{t}\!\bigl(L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}}\bigr)\;-\;\rho_{t}\!\bigl(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}_{t}(h_{t})),\pi^{+}}\bigr). (2)

We write ct+​(a):=max⁡{ct​(a),0}c_{t}^{+}(a):=\max\{c_{t}(a),0\} for the runtime charge under the convention that risk-reducing actions are not subsidised.

Theorem 8 (Time-consistent counterfactual tolls).

Under Assumptions 3–4 and the recursion (1), the dynamic risk process is time-consistent: for every 0≤t<s≤T0\leq t<s\leq T, if ρs​(X)≤ρs​(Y)\rho_{s}(X)\leq\rho_{s}(Y) a.s. then ρt​(X)≤ρt​(Y)\rho_{t}(X)\leq\rho_{t}(Y) a.s. Moreover, for every well-posed action a∈𝒜t​(ht)a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}), the toll ct​(a∣ht;π+)c_{t}(a\mid h_{t};\pi^{+}) in (2) is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable and bounded. If Ldo⁡(a),π+≤Ldo⁡(b),π+L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}}\leq L^{\operatorname{do}(b),\pi^{+}} a.s. for two actions a,ba,b, then ρt​(Ldo⁡(a),π+)≤ρt​(Ldo⁡(b),π+)\rho_{t}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}})\leq\rho_{t}(L^{\operatorname{do}(b),\pi^{+}}).

Proof sketch.

By backward induction. Each σs\sigma_{s} maps Lp​(ℱs+1)→Lp​(ℱs)L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{s+1})\to L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{s}), so starting from ρT​(X)=X∈Lp​(ℱT)\rho_{T}(X)=X\in L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{T}) and applying σT−1,…,σt\sigma_{T-1},\ldots,\sigma_{t}, we obtain ρt​(X)∈Lp​(ℱt)\rho_{t}(X)\in L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{t}); in particular, ρt​(X)\rho_{t}(X) is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable. For dynamic consistency, suppose ρs​(X)≤ρs​(Y)\rho_{s}(X)\leq\rho_{s}(Y) a.s.; then monotonicity of σs−1\sigma_{s-1} (Assumption 4(ii)) gives ρs−1​(X)=σs−1​(ρs​(X))≤σs−1​(ρs​(Y))=ρs−1​(Y)\rho_{s-1}(X)=\sigma_{s-1}(\rho_{s}(X))\leq\sigma_{s-1}(\rho_{s}(Y))=\rho_{s-1}(Y) a.s. Iterating from ss down to tt yields the claim. The toll ctc_{t} is the ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable difference of two Lp​(ℱt)L^{p}(\mathcal{F}_{t}) random variables and is bounded by translation invariance: |ct​(a)|≤‖Ldo⁡(a),π+‖∞+‖Ldo⁡(a0),π+‖∞|c_{t}(a)|\leq\|L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}}\|_{\infty}+\|L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}),\pi^{+}}\|_{\infty} when p=∞p=\infty. The dominance claim follows from dynamic consistency with s=Ts=T and ρT​(X)=X\rho_{T}(X)=X. No uniqueness of the toll is used; it is well-defined only after fixing (a0,π+,ρ,ℬ,ℳ)(a^{0},\pi^{+},\rho,\mathcal{B},\mathcal{M}). ∎

Remark 9 (No uniqueness claim).

Theorem 8 does not claim that {ct}\{c_{t}\} is the unique actuarial decomposition of ρ0​(L)\rho_{0}(L) satisfying any prescribed axiom set; competing decompositions (e.g. Shapley-style or martingale-based) are admissible. The toll is a well-defined, time-consistent, counterfactual decomposition once the five primitives are fixed.

5 No-Splitting within an Underwriting Boundary

Let ΦB:ℝ+d→ℝ+\Phi_{B}:\mathbb{R}^{d}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} be a monotone toll potential with ΦB​(0)=0\Phi_{B}(0)=0. Define the boundary-level toll

λt​(at∣EtB,B)=ΦB​(EtB+Δ​EtB​(at))−ΦB​(EtB).\lambda_{t}\bigl(a_{t}\mid E^{B}_{t},B\bigr)\;=\;\Phi_{B}\bigl(E^{B}_{t}+\Delta E^{B}_{t}(a_{t})\bigr)-\Phi_{B}\bigl(E^{B}_{t}\bigr). (3)

The boundary toll is the operational realisation of ctc_{t} when the conditional loss law given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} depends on within-BB history only through EtBE^{B}_{t}; the calibration of ΦB\Phi_{B} to ρt\rho_{t} is treated in Paper B.

Assumption 10 (Boundary-determined conditional loss).

Inside boundary BB, the conditional law of LL given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} depends on the within-BB action history only through the cumulative exposure EtBE^{B}_{t} and an outside state variable ξt\xi_{t}: ℙ(L∈⋅∣ℱt)=ℙ(L∈⋅∣EtB,ξt)\mathbb{P}(L\in\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t})=\mathbb{P}(L\in\cdot\mid E^{B}_{t},\xi_{t}). The variable ξt\xi_{t} is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable, encodes state outside BB that is relevant to the priced conditional law, and is not reset by splitting an action into smaller increments, opening new sessions, re-labelling equivalent actions, or routing through proxy agents. The non-reset property is part of the contract definition of ξt\xi_{t}; it fails by default for naive boundary designs and is the principal obligation of boundary calibration.

Theorem 11 (No-splitting within an underwriting boundary).

Fix a boundary BB satisfying Assumptions 6–10. For any finite sequence of within-BB side-effect actions (a0,…,aT−1)(a_{0},\ldots,a_{T-1}) with exposure dynamics Et+1B=EtB+Δ​EtB​(at)E^{B}_{t+1}=E^{B}_{t}+\Delta E^{B}_{t}(a_{t}), the total boundary toll generated by (3) satisfies

∑t=0T−1λt​(at∣EtB,B)=ΦB​(ETB)−ΦB​(E0B).\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\lambda_{t}(a_{t}\mid E^{B}_{t},B)\;=\;\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{T})-\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{0}).

In particular, any decomposition of the same cumulative exposure increment ETB−E0BE^{B}_{T}-E^{B}_{0} into smaller actions within the same boundary pays the same total toll. If ΦB\Phi_{B} is convex and nondecreasing, concentrating exposure into higher cumulative states cannot reduce total toll relative to the terminal cumulative-exposure charge.

Proof sketch.

Substitute the dynamics Et+1B=EtB+Δ​EtB​(at)E^{B}_{t+1}=E^{B}_{t}+\Delta E^{B}_{t}(a_{t}) into (3) to get λt=ΦB​(Et+1B)−ΦB​(EtB)\lambda_{t}=\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{t+1})-\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{t}), then telescope: ∑t=0T−1[ΦB​(Et+1B)−ΦB​(EtB)]=ΦB​(ETB)−ΦB​(E0B)\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}[\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{t+1})-\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{t})]=\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{T})-\Phi_{B}(E^{B}_{0}). The total depends on (E0B,ETB)(E^{B}_{0},E^{B}_{T}) alone, hence is invariant under within-BB decomposition. Convexity of ΦB\Phi_{B} is not required for the identity; it becomes material when the designer wants the marginal toll to increase with cumulative exposure. If Assumption 10 fails, LL admits a path-dependent component beyond ETBE^{B}_{T} which ΦB\Phi_{B} cannot capture, and adversarial sequencing can strictly reduce realised toll within BB. Cross-boundary arbitrage is not blocked by Theorem 11 and must be addressed by boundary design (Corollary 12). ∎

Corollary 12 (Boundary design as gaming-resistance).

Theorem 11 prevents splitting only within a fixed observable boundary whose state (EtB,ξt)(E^{B}_{t},\xi_{t}) is sufficient for the relevant conditional loss law. Cross-session, cross-entity, path-dependent, ξt\xi_{t}-relabel, and proxy-agent arbitrage are not automatically blocked; they must be handled by boundary design, including common-control aggregation, rolling time windows, related-party rules, action-category linking, currency and asset normalisation, and audit rules that prevent the operator from resetting ξt\xi_{t} by relabelling economically equivalent actions. If Assumption 10 fails inside BB, gaming-resistance reduces to redesigning BB so the assumption holds for the contractually insured loss class.

6 Irreversible Authority Premium

We compare two authority sets 𝒜t0​(ht)⊂𝒜t+​(ht)=𝒜t0​(ht)∪{a+}\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}(h_{t})\subset\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}(h_{t})=\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}(h_{t})\cup\{a^{+}\}. We work under an ambiguity set ℳ\mathcal{M} of admissible environment models, with ρtM\rho_{t}^{M} denoting the dynamic risk under model M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M}.

Definition 13 (Uncompensated irreversible tail exposure).

The action a+a^{+} creates uncompensated irreversible tail exposure relative to safe default a0a^{0} at history hth_{t} if there exist a model M⋆∈ℳM^{\star}\in\mathcal{M}, an event G∈ℱTG\in\mathcal{F}_{T} with ℙM⋆​(G∣ht)>0\mathbb{P}^{M^{\star}}(G\mid h_{t})>0, and constants δ>0\delta>0, η<δ\eta<\delta such that:

  1. (i)

    Tail-loss gap. Ldo⁡(a+),π+≥Ldo⁡(a0),π+L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}}\geq L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}),\pi^{+}} a.s. under M⋆M^{\star}, and Ldo⁡(a+),π+≥Ldo⁡(a0),π++δL^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}}\geq L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}),\pi^{+}}+\delta on GG under M⋆M^{\star}.

  2. (ii)

    Irreversibility. No admissible continuation policy can reduce the loss gap on GG by more than η<δ\eta<\delta.

  3. (iii)

    Strict ρ\rho-monotonicity for this pair under M⋆M^{\star}. A terminal-loss change that is weakly nonnegative a.s. and strictly positive on GG produces a strictly higher value of ρtM⋆\rho_{t}^{M^{\star}} at the current history.

The three conditions are logically independent: (i) alone leaves room for the gap to be erased by continuation, (i)+(ii) without (iii) leaves the gap invisible to the risk mapping, and (i)+(iii) without (ii) leaves the gap hedgeable.

Define the action-level authority premium and the set-level robust capital:

Δt​(a+∣ht)\displaystyle\Delta_{t}(a^{+}\mid h_{t}) :=supM∈ℳ[ρtM​(Ldo⁡(a+),π+)−ρtM​(Ldo⁡(a0),π+)]+,\displaystyle\;:=\;\sup_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\bigl[\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}})-\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}),\pi^{+}})\bigr]_{+}, (4)
Kt​(U∣ht)\displaystyle K_{t}(U\mid h_{t}) :=supM∈ℳsupa∈UρtM​(Ldo⁡(a),π+),U⊆𝒜t​(ht).\displaystyle\;:=\;\sup_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\sup_{a\in U}\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}}),\quad U\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{t}(h_{t}). (5)
Theorem 14 (Irreversible authority premium).

Suppose 𝒜t+​(ht)=𝒜t0​(ht)∪{a+}\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}(h_{t})=\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}(h_{t})\cup\{a^{+}\}, the relevant robust risks are finite (so that Kt​(𝒜t+∣ht)<∞K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}\mid h_{t})<\infty and the supremum defining Δt​(a+∣ht)\Delta_{t}(a^{+}\mid h_{t}) is finite), and a+a^{+} creates uncompensated irreversible tail exposure relative to its safe default a0a^{0} in the sense of Definition 13. Then:

  1. (a)

    Action-level premium is strictly positive: Δt​(a+∣ht)>0\Delta_{t}(a^{+}\mid h_{t})>0.

  2. (b)

    Set-level capital increase is conditional: Kt​(𝒜t+​(ht)∣ht)>Kt​(𝒜t0​(ht)∣ht)K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}(h_{t})\mid h_{t})>K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}(h_{t})\mid h_{t}) if and only if

    supM∈ℳρtM​(Ldo⁡(a+),π+)>Kt​(𝒜t0​(ht)∣ht).\sup_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\rho_{t}^{M}\bigl(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}}\bigr)\;>\;K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}(h_{t})\mid h_{t}).
Proof sketch.

Action-level (a). Pick the witness M⋆M^{\star} of Definition 13. Set X=Ldo⁡(a+),π+X=L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}} and Y=Ldo⁡(a0),π+Y=L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{0}),\pi^{+}}. Condition (i) gives X≥YX\geq Y a.s. under M⋆M^{\star} and X≥Y+δX\geq Y+\delta on GG. Condition (ii) ensures the gap on GG cannot be erased by continuation policy, so even after admissible modification of π+\pi^{+} on the post-tt trajectory we retain X≥Y+(δ−η)>YX\geq Y+(\delta-\eta)>Y on GG with positive probability. Condition (iii) yields strict ρ\rho-monotonicity for this pair: ρtM⋆​(X)>ρtM⋆​(Y)\rho_{t}^{M^{\star}}(X)>\rho_{t}^{M^{\star}}(Y). Therefore Δt​(a+∣ht)≥[ρtM⋆​(X)−ρtM⋆​(Y)]+>0\Delta_{t}(a^{+}\mid h_{t})\geq[\rho_{t}^{M^{\star}}(X)-\rho_{t}^{M^{\star}}(Y)]_{+}>0.

Set-level (b). Since 𝒜t+=𝒜t0∪{a+}\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}=\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}\cup\{a^{+}\}, for each M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} we have supa∈𝒜t+ρtM​(Ldo⁡(a),π+)=max⁡(supa∈𝒜t0ρtM​(Ldo⁡(a),π+),ρtM​(Ldo⁡(a+),π+))\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}}\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}})=\max\bigl(\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}}\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a),\pi^{+}}),\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}})\bigr). Using supMmax⁡(f,g)=max⁡(supMf,supMg)\sup_{M}\max(f,g)=\max(\sup_{M}f,\sup_{M}g),

Kt​(𝒜t+∣ht)=max⁡(Kt​(𝒜t0∣ht),supM∈ℳρtM​(Ldo⁡(a+),π+)).K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t}\mid h_{t})\;=\;\max\!\Bigl(K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}\mid h_{t}),\;\sup_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\rho_{t}^{M}(L^{\operatorname{do}(a^{+}),\pi^{+}})\Bigr).

Strict greater than Kt​(𝒜t0∣ht)K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}\mid h_{t}) iff the second argument strictly exceeds the first, proving (b) as an if-and-only-if. ∎

Remark 15 (Why the split matters).

Without distinguishing Δt\Delta_{t} from KtK_{t}, the naive claim “adding an irreversible action raises robust capital” is false: if 𝒜t0\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t} already permits an action whose worst-case risk exceeds that of a+a^{+}, then Kt​(𝒜t+)=Kt​(𝒜t0)K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{+}_{t})=K_{t}(\mathcal{A}^{0}_{t}). The defensible content is that irreversible non-hedgeable authority has a strictly positive incremental price relative to its own safe default, and additionally raises contract-level capital only when it becomes binding. This decomposition mirrors the distinction between marginal and total risk contributions in classical capital allocation [20].

7 Runtime Risk Gating with Conservative Upper Bounds

Exact computation of ct​(a∣ht)c_{t}(a\mid h_{t}) at every action is prohibitive in deployment. Let c¯t​(a∣ht)\bar{c}_{t}(a\mid h_{t}) be a conservative nonnegative upper envelope on the positive toll ct+​(a∣ht)c_{t}^{+}(a\mid h_{t}), provided by simulation, a calibrated quantile model, or distributionally robust optimisation.

Assumption 16 (High-probability toll envelope).

Fix a confidence level 1−δ∈(0,1)1-\delta\in(0,1). The envelope c¯t≥0\bar{c}_{t}\geq 0 on a set of adaptively evaluated query points ℐ⊆{(t,at)}\mathcal{I}\subseteq\{(t,a_{t})\} satisfies

ℙ⁡(ct+​(at∣ht)≤c¯t​(at∣ht)​ for all ​(t,at)∈ℐ)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\,c_{t}^{+}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\leq\bar{c}_{t}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\text{ for all }(t,a_{t})\in\mathcal{I}\right)\geq 1-\delta.

For envelopes constructed by conformal prediction, the calibration scheme must match the deployment adaptivity assumptions: split conformal [21, 2] is sufficient under exchangeable or fixed evaluation, while online adaptive action selection—in which the policy itself depends on c¯\bar{c}—generally breaks exchangeability and requires an online or adaptive conformal variant [11].

Theorem 17 (Runtime risk-budget guarantee).

Let an agent begin with toll budget B0≥0B_{0}\geq 0. A runtime gate executes action ata_{t} at time tt only if

c¯t​(at∣ht)≤Bt,\bar{c}_{t}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\leq B_{t},

in which case the budget is updated Bt+1:=Bt−c¯t​(at∣ht)B_{t+1}:=B_{t}-\bar{c}_{t}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}); otherwise the gate blocks, downgrades to safe default at0​(ht)a^{0}_{t}(h_{t}), or escalates to human approval. Under Assumption 16, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

∑(t,at)∈ℐexecct+​(at∣ht)≤B0,\sum_{(t,a_{t})\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{exec}}}c_{t}^{+}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\;\leq\;B_{0},

where ℐexec\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{exec}} is the set of gate-admitted executed actions.

Proof sketch.

Let ℰδ={ct+(at∣ht)≤c¯t(at∣ht) for all (t,at)∈ℐ}\mathcal{E}_{\delta}=\{c_{t}^{+}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\leq\bar{c}_{t}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\text{ for all }(t,a_{t})\in\mathcal{I}\}; by Assumption 16, ℙ⁡(ℰδ)≥1−δ\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\delta})\geq 1-\delta. Work on ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}. The gate executes only when c¯t≤Bt\bar{c}_{t}\leq B_{t} and updates Bt+1=Bt−c¯tB_{t+1}=B_{t}-\bar{c}_{t}. Since c¯t≥0\bar{c}_{t}\geq 0, the budget recursion is monotone-nonincreasing, Bt≥0B_{t}\geq 0 throughout, and summing across executed actions gives

∑(t,at)∈ℐexecc¯t​(at∣ht)=B0−Bfinal≤B0.\sum_{(t,a_{t})\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{exec}}}\bar{c}_{t}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\;=\;B_{0}-B_{\mathrm{final}}\;\leq\;B_{0}.

On ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, ct+≤c¯tc_{t}^{+}\leq\bar{c}_{t} on every evaluated point, hence on every executed point, so ∑ct+≤∑c¯t≤B0\sum c_{t}^{+}\leq\sum\bar{c}_{t}\leq B_{0}. All statistical difficulty is isolated in the validity of Assumption 16 under the deployment adaptivity regime. ∎

Remark 18 (Why this paper does not claim policy dominance).

A tempting stronger claim is that adding tolls makes the agent’s terminal-loss distribution first-order stochastically dominate the untolled baseline. That claim is false in a general MDP for at least three reasons: (a) the reward may be perversely correlated with tail loss, so risk-toll-induced changes to the policy can shift mass to worse outcomes elsewhere; (b) the action space may lack any lower-risk substitute for the priced action under the relevant history, so the penalised policy collapses to refusal rather than substitution; (c) local one-step risk-toll penalties need not imply global distributional dominance even when monotone in expectation. The defensible structural statement of this framework is the budget guarantee (Theorem 17). Any policy-improvement result should be stated either as an empirical Paper B outcome or under explicit reward–loss alignment and action-richness assumptions, following the risk-sensitive MDP literature [9, 19].

8 Companion Layers and Program Interfaces

The preceding sections define the foundational contract objects: the side-effect-bearing action, the minimal-authority safe default, the underwriting boundary, the counterfactual toll, the boundary potential, the irreversible-authority premium, and the conservative gate. The rest of the research program keeps those primitives fixed and asks three different questions.

This division prevents the foundational claims from becoming overbroad. Paper A does not claim that tolls make every policy safer, that a finite benchmark exhausts agent risk, or that strategic manipulation is impossible without additional contract clauses. It claims the narrower accounting facts proved above: the toll is well-defined once primitives are fixed, within-boundary splitting telescopes through a boundary potential, irreversible authority has positive marginal price when the stated witness conditions hold, and a gate that charges a valid conservative envelope cannot spend more positive toll than its initial budget on the covered execution path.

Empirical status.

The empirical companion [7] has moved beyond the original deterministic database prototype. It instantiates the same safe-default and budget recursion through a deterministic runtime interface, paired proposal-replay experiments, Postgres/LangChain stress tests, four-environment authority-frontier summaries, and a live LLM underwriting panel. Those results are intentionally not re-reported here; their role is to test the operational relevance of the mathematical objects introduced in this paper.

9 Residual Obligations and Scope

The proof sketches above isolate the assumptions under which the four foundational results hold. The following obligations remain outside the scope of this paper, or are handled by companion layers rather than by changing the present theorems:

  1. 1.

    Model-class verification. Strict ρ\rho-monotonicity for the witness pair under M⋆M^{\star} (Definition 13(iii)) must be verified for any chosen runtime risk family. The entropic family and conditional ESα\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha} require separate verification of their strictness regimes.

  2. 2.

    Closed-loop calibration. Assumption 16 is a high-probability envelope assumption. Split conformal methods supply it under exchangeability; closed-loop deployment requires an online-valid or audit-replay calibration protocol [11]. The dynamic-underwriting companion develops one audit-replay route, but this paper does not prove a general adversarial conformal theorem.

  3. 3.

    Boundary failure and cross-boundary settlement. Theorem 11 is strictly within-boundary. Cross-session, related-party, proxy-agent, and multi-boundary arbitrage require explicit aggregate settlement clauses. These are mechanism-design questions built on top of Corollary 12, not hidden consequences of Theorem 11.

  4. 4.

    Policy welfare. Theorem 17 is a reserve accounting guarantee, not a welfare theorem and not a first-order stochastic dominance statement. Any claim that tolls improve outcomes requires empirical evidence or additional reward–loss alignment and action-richness assumptions.
